lesson.title: When Genes Travel Together: The Exception to Independent Assortment
lesson.summary: Genes located close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited as a package rather than independently, a pattern called genetic linkage that violates Mendel's law of independent assortment unless crossing over breaks the linkage.
lesson.body:
Recall Mendel's law of independent assortment: alleles of different genes sort into gametes independently of one another, producing the classic 9:3:3:1 ratio in a dihybrid cross. That law works beautifully when the two genes sit on different chromosomes, because each pair of homologous chromosomes lines up and separates independently during meiosis I. But Mendel got lucky. Several of the seven pea traits he studied happen to sit far apart on their chromosomes or on different chromosomes entirely, so independent assortment held up. Most genes are not so conveniently spaced.

When two genes sit close together on the same chromosome, they tend to travel together into the same gamete, simply because they are physically attached to the same DNA molecule. This is genetic linkage. Instead of shuffling independently, linked alleles are inherited as a unit far more often than chance would predict, and a dihybrid cross between linked genes no longer produces a 9:3:3:1 ratio. The closer two genes sit, the more tightly linked they are and the less often they separate.

Linkage is not absolute, though, because of genetic recombination during meiosis I. When homologous chromosomes pair up in prophase I, non-sister chromatids can physically cross over and exchange segments of DNA. If a crossover happens to occur between the two linked genes, it can separate alleles that started out on the same chromosome and combine them onto a new chromatid, alongside alleles from the other homolog. Offspring that inherit these swapped combinations are called recombinants, while offspring that inherit the original, unswapped combinations are called parental types.

A test cross reveals linkage clearly. Suppose a fly heterozygous for two genes, body color (A dominant, a recessive) and wing shape (B dominant, b recessive), arranged on the same chromosome as A B slash a b, is crossed with a fly that is homozygous recessive for both traits, a b slash a b. If the genes assorted independently, the test cross should yield four phenotype classes in a 1:1:1:1 ratio, each at 25 percent. Instead, imagine the cross produces 1000 offspring: 440 with the AaBb parental phenotype, 440 with the aabb parental phenotype, and only 60 with the Aabb recombinant phenotype and 60 with the aaBb recombinant phenotype. The parental classes vastly outnumber the recombinant classes, a signature of linkage. The two genes are clearly not assorting independently, and the relatively small number of recombinants tells us a crossover between them is uncommon, which in turn tells us the genes must be close together. That relationship between recombinant frequency and physical distance is exactly what the next chapter turns into a precise measurement.
